strengths: Addresses an underexplored and practically important problem: image-level online data curation for object detection, motivated by the well-documented difficulty of using loss-based learnability signals in detection due to fragmented, architecture-dependent loss terms.

Technically interesting formulation that reframes learnability as the marginal contribution of an image to dataset-level (non-decomposable) AP, derived analytically via a Stieltjes-integral treatment of the PR curve, with closed-form solutions under a uniform-prior simplification that enables O(1)/O(m) per-image scoring.

The closed-form approximation is validated against Monte Carlo simulation (Appendix 4) and against detector-specific Beta-fitted priors (Appendix 6), showing the simplification preserves ranking quality while being far cheaper, which strengthens the credibility of the core technical claim.

Broad empirical validation across six architecturally diverse detectors (two-stage, one-stage anchor-based/free, transformer-based) with consistent mAP gains (~+1.6 to +2.7), plus systematic ablations on sampling ratio, teacher capacity/architecture family, robustness to annotation noise, and pseudo-labeled data.

Extensive comparison against many alternative online sampling criteria (loss-based, gradient-based, entropy/diversity-based, an existing image-level AP metric) under matched pipelines, showing DetGain is more stable across detector families.
Demonstrates practical complementarity with knowledge distillation and shows the method is non-intrusive (data-pipeline only), which increases its potential usefulness and ease of adoption.

Good transparency about limitations (training overhead, naive augmentation) and reasonably detailed implementation/reproducibility information (algorithm, pseudocode, augmentation configuration tables) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core efficiency argument rests on strong simplifying assumptions: a uniform Beta(1,1) prior for TP/FP score distributions and a first-order additive approximation for aggregating per-detection and per-image contributions into batch/dataset-level ΔmAP. While Appendix 6 shows comparable validation performance versus a model-specific prior, this is only tested for one detector (Faster R-CNN), leaving open whether the approximation holds equally well across all six architectures reported in the main results.

Training overhead is significant (up to ~2.4-3x wall-clock at the recommended 20% sampling ratio) for modest accuracy gains (~2 mAP on average); the paper doesn't fully quantify the total added compute cost (including teacher pretraining, which requires a separately trained larger-backbone model) relative to simply training longer or using a larger student, weakening the data-efficiency narrative.

All experiments are conducted solely on COCO; no results on other detection benchmarks (e.g., LVIS for long-tail claims, Objects365, Pascal VOC, or a different domain) are provided to support claims of general applicability across long-tailed distributions and diverse domains.

No reported variance across multiple runs/seeds; given that several reported gains are in the 1-3 mAP range, the absence of error bars or repeated trials makes it hard to assess statistical significance, particularly for the smaller gains in Table 1 and Table 3.

The teacher must be from the same architecture family for good results (Appendix 1 shows asynchronous teacher-student pairing hurts performance substantially), which somewhat limits the claimed architecture-agnostic generality and increases the practical burden of maintaining matched larger-backbone teachers per detector family.

The per-detection additive independence assumption used both within an image (aggregating over multiple simultaneous detections) and across a selected mini-batch (Section 3.1's additive approximation) is asserted rather than empirically validated at the batch level actually used in training (top-16 of 80), only justified as O(|B|/|D|) which is a dataset-level argument, not a rigorous check that per-image marginal effects don't interact substantially within a curated sub-batch.

The comparison table for alternative sampling metrics (Table 5) covers only three detectors, while the main results table covers six, creating an inconsistency in evaluation breadth across different claims.

Presentation could be improved: notation is dense across Sections 3.1-3.2, and some contribution framing (e.g., 'the first' image-wise online sampling with measurable detection gains) is a strong claim that slightly overstates novelty given prior related work such as [61] is acknowledged as addressing a similar idea offline.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: online, model-aware data curation for object detection, where prior learnability-based curation methods (RHO-LOSS, JEST, ACED) have focused on classification/multimodal settings and do not transfer cleanly due to detection's fragmented, matching-dependent losses.

The core idea of scoring images by their estimated marginal contribution to dataset-level AP rather than by raw loss is conceptually sound and better aligned with the evaluation metric than loss-based learnability signals.

Solid mathematical derivation of the closed-form marginal AP perturbation under a TP/FP score-distribution model, with an independent Monte Carlo verification (Appendix 4) that lends credibility to the analytic approximation.

Reasonably broad empirical validation: six detector families (two-stage, one-stage anchor-based/free, and transformer-based) are tested, along with ablations on teacher backbone, sampling ratio, prior distribution choice, and robustness to label noise and pseudo-labels.

The comparison against several alternative online-selection baselines (GradNorm, hard-example mining, entropy-based AL criteria, image-wise AP) in a unified framework is a useful contribution to understanding which signals are stable across architectures.
Combining DetGain with knowledge distillation and demonstrating complementarity (Table 6) is an interesting and practically relevant finding.
weaknesses: The uniform-prior simplification (Beta(1,1)) reduces the elaborate PR-curve perturbation framework to a function depending only on aggregate counts (T, F) and the detection's own score s, discarding essentially all information about the actual score distribution; the paper does not convincingly justify why this heavy machinery is necessary when the final deployed estimator is this simple, nor fully reconcile this with the motivating narrative about modeling global score distributions.

The method strongly resembles implicit self/cross-distillation: the teacher is a larger model of the same architecture family trained on the *same* labeled training set, and DetGain alone (Table 6) achieves gains comparable to full KD methods (PKD, CrossKD) that explicitly transfer feature-level knowledge. This raises the concern that much of the reported benefit is a distillation effect mediated through data selection rather than a genuine "informativeness" signal distinct from teacher quality, which is not sufficiently disentangled.

No iso-compute or iso-wall-clock baseline is reported. The method incurs ~2.4–3x training-time overhead (Table 4), yet the main comparisons (Table 1, Table 5) are iteration-matched rather than compute-matched against simply training the baseline (or baseline+augmentation) longer with the saved compute budget, leaving open whether the gains would persist under a fair compute budget.

Gains are modest and inconsistent in the augmentation-only ablation: strong augmentation alone sometimes hurts performance (ATSS -0.8, FCOS 0.0, GFL -... , VFNet -0.4 mAP), suggesting the augmentation recipe is not well-tuned on its own, which complicates attributing improvement cleanly to the DetGain sampling mechanism versus augmentation-selection interaction.

Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (COCO); no cross-domain or cross-dataset generalization experiments (e.g., different object scales/domains such as aerial or medical imagery) are provided to support the claimed architecture- and domain-agnostic generality.

No variance/error bars across multiple runs are reported for the main results, making it hard to assess whether the reported 1–3 mAP gains are statistically robust rather than run-to-run noise, especially given the many moving hyperparameters (augmentation strength per detector family, sampling ratio, super-batch size) that appear to be manually tuned per architecture.

The practical overhead argument ("deployed model remains unchanged, so extra training compute is an offline investment") downplays training cost, which is a central concern in the scale-law/data-efficiency framing the paper itself adopts in the introduction; this internal tension is not well addressed.

Novelty relative to prior AP-based offline metric-driven selection [61] and the teacher-student learnability framework [14,15,37] is incremental; the main innovation is the closed-form online estimator plus the uniform-prior trick, which, while convenient, somewhat limits the conceptual contribution.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and underexplored gap: existing online/learnability-based data curation methods rely on loss signals that are unstable in object detection due to heterogeneous, architecture-dependent loss compositions (RPN sampling, Hungarian matching, etc.), and proposes a metric-aware alternative tied directly to the evaluation metric (mAP).

The core technical contribution (closed-form marginal AP change from inserting a TP/FP under a maximum-entropy/uniform score prior) is mathematically well-derived, with full derivations provided in the appendix and cross-checked against Monte Carlo simulation (Fig. 5), which is a good and often-missing verification practice.

Broad experimental coverage across six architecturally diverse detectors (two-stage, one-stage anchor-based/free, transformer-based), consistently showing improvements, which supports the claim of architecture-agnosticism.

Extensive and thoughtful ablations: teacher backbone/family choice, sampling ratio vs. cost trade-off, robustness under multiple types of synthetic label noise and pseudo-labels, comparison to a substantial number of alternative online sampling metrics (loss/gradient/entropy/image-AP based), and complementarity with knowledge distillation.
The method is minimally intrusive (data-pipeline only), requiring no changes to loss, architecture, or optimizer, which increases practical usefulness and ease of adoption.
Good transparency about limitations (added training overhead, simplicity of augmentation choices) and inclusion of implementation-level pseudocode/algorithm for reproducibility.
weaknesses: All main results (Table 1) report '+DetGain' as the combination of strong augmentation and DetGain-based sampling together, making it hard from that table alone to isolate the sampling method's individual contribution; the disentangling analysis (Table 2) is only provided for a single detector (Faster R-CNN), leaving open whether the augmentation+curation interaction generalizes as cleanly to the other five architectures.

The reported training-time overhead is substantial (up to ~2.4-3x wall-clock at the adopted 20% sampling ratio) for scoring passes; while inference cost is unaffected, this cost is non-trivial for practitioners and is not deeply analyzed for very large-scale or long-schedule training regimes.

The core estimator relies on collapsing all TP/FP score distributions to a maximum-entropy Beta(1,1) uniform prior; although the appendix shows negligible difference vs. a fitted Faster R-CNN-specific prior, this comparison is done for only one detector/teacher pairing, so it remains unclear how well the uniform-prior simplification holds for very different score-distribution shapes (e.g., transformer-based detectors with different confidence calibration).

Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (COCO); no results are shown on other benchmarks (e.g., different domains, long-tailed datasets like LVIS, or smaller-scale datasets), which would strengthen claims of general applicability.

The teacher must generally come from the same architecture family for best results (Appendix Table 7), which somewhat limits the claimed 'architecture-agnostic' flexibility of the method in practice, since a same-family larger-backbone teacher is not always readily available.
No variance/multiple-seed reporting is provided for the main results, so the statistical reliability of the reported (often modest, 1.5-3 mAP) gains cannot be fully assessed.

The additive first-order approximation for combining per-detection and per-image marginal AP contributions (assuming b ≪ D) is a reasonable engineering choice but is not empirically stress-tested against the true non-additive/ranking-based AP computation at larger sub-batch fractions beyond the sampling-ratio ablation.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: online, image-level data curation for object detection, motivated by real limitations (loss instability from Hungarian matching/RPN sampling, heterogeneous multi-task losses) that make classification-style teacher-student loss-gap learnability inapplicable.

Solid theoretical derivation: the paper derives a closed-form Stieltjes-integral expression for the marginal change in AP from inserting a single TP/FP detection, and further simplifies it under a uniform (maximum-entropy) score prior to obtain an O(1) analytic estimator per detection. This derivation is carried through in detail in the appendix and cross-checked against Monte Carlo simulation (Fig. 7) with excellent agreement.

Broad and fairly rigorous empirical validation: results across six detector families (two-stage, one-stage anchor-based/free, DETR-style), consistent gains (~+2.0 mAP average, up to +2.7), multiple seeds with reported std, extensive ablations (teacher backbone/family, uniform vs. fitted prior, additivity assumption validity vs. base-set size), robustness under synthetic label noise and pseudo-labels, and comparisons against many alternative online sampling criteria (loss-based, gradient-based, entropy/diversity, image-AP) where DetGain is consistently more stable.

Demonstrates complementarity with orthogonal techniques: combination with strong augmentation (addressing overfitting from pure learnability-based subsampling) and with knowledge distillation methods (PKD, CrossKD), showing additive benefits and lower sensitivity to teacher strength than KD.

Method is architecture-agnostic and non-intrusive (post-hoc on detection outputs), and the appendix provides substantial reproducibility support: algorithm pseudocode, augmentation configuration tables, runtime/memory overhead analysis, and validation on additional datasets (VOC, BDD100K).
weaknesses: A critical practical detail is under-specified: how are the dataset-level counts (T_{c,τ}, F_{c,τ}, T^GT_c) used inside the closed-form estimator actually computed/updated online at each training iteration across the full ~118K-image COCO training set? The paper does not clearly describe whether these are recomputed per-iteration, cached/updated periodically, or approximated, which is central to both correctness and the claimed real-time feasibility of the method.

Non-trivial computational overhead: Appendix 8 shows iteration time roughly tripling (0.25s→0.75s) with a naive implementation, plus ~53% higher CPU memory from buffering larger super-batches and extra teacher/student forward passes; while a dynamic-ratio mitigation is proposed, the core method's cost-efficiency claims ("data-efficient") are undercut by this overhead, and the teacher itself requires separate pretraining not counted in the reported efficiency comparisons.

The "+Data Aug." baseline sometimes hurts performance (e.g., ATSS −0.8, VFNet −0.4 AP@50), and the augmentation strengths/probabilities are manually tuned per detector family (Appendix 5), raising a fairness concern about whether the augmentation baseline was optimally tuned, since DetGain's reported gain partly rests on "filtering out low-quality augmentations" relative to this baseline.

Evaluation of scalability is limited: all main experiments use ResNet-50 students, and datasets tested (COCO, VOC, BDD100K) are moderate scale; no evaluation on more extreme long-tailed or larger-category benchmarks (e.g., LVIS, Objects365) where the per-class T/F statistics used in the estimator would be much sparser and noisier for rare classes.

Minor inconsistencies between tables (e.g., Faster R-CNN uniform baseline AP is 37.5 in Table 1 but 37.3 in Table 4) suggest either different runs or rounding that is not clearly explained, slightly undermining precision of comparisons.

The first-order additive approximation for batch-level ΔmAP and the uniform-prior simplification are reasonable engineering choices but are still approximations whose quality is only validated via simulation under assumed detector-fitted or synthetic priors rather than being fully characterized during actual noisy early-training dynamics where score distributions are far from converged.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: online, teacher-student data curation has succeeded in classification/multimodal learning but rarely in object detection due to loss instability; the paper identifies this clearly and motivates a metric-aligned alternative.

Technically rigorous derivation: the paper derives closed-form marginal ΔAP contributions for TP/FP insertions from first principles (Stieltjes integral formulation), and importantly validates these derivations both analytically (Appendix 3) and empirically via Monte Carlo simulation (Appendix 4), which is a level of self-verification rarely seen in similar papers.

Broad architecture coverage: experiments span two-stage, one-stage anchor-based/anchor-free, and DETR-based detectors (6 architectures total), showing the method generalizes across loss formulations and training paradigms.

Extensive and well-designed ablations: uniform vs. fitted prior comparison with Spearman correlation analysis, teacher backbone/architecture sensitivity (including a negative result for asynchronous architectures, showing honesty), robustness under controlled annotation noise and pseudo-labels, and comparisons against a wide range of alternative selection metrics (loss-based, gradient-based, entropy-based, image-AP).

Practical considerations are addressed: computational overhead is explicitly measured and a dynamic sampling-ratio schedule is proposed to mitigate it; combination with knowledge distillation is explored, showing complementarity rather than redundancy.
Additional validation beyond COCO (VOC, BDD100K) and demonstration of faster convergence (Fig. 9) strengthens the practical usefulness case.
The method is architecture-agnostic and non-intrusive (data-pipeline only), which is a meaningful practical advantage over KD or loss-modification approaches.
weaknesses: The core scoring relies on several stacked approximations (uniform TP/FP score prior, first-order additivity of per-image ΔAP, one-to-one IoU matching per threshold); while each is individually validated, the cumulative effect of these approximations on the fidelity of the actual (non-ranking) DetGain values is not fully characterized, and the paper leans heavily on rank-correlation arguments to justify them.

The reported computational overhead is substantial in the naive implementation (iteration time roughly 3x baseline in the VOC case), and while the dynamic-ratio schedule mitigates this, the primary COCO results in Table 1 do not report wall-clock or overhead numbers alongside the accuracy gains, making it hard to judge the practical cost-benefit trade-off for the main experiments.

Teacher effectiveness is shown to depend on same-architecture-family pretraining (Appendix 1), which somewhat weakens the claimed architecture-agnostic generality, since a same-family stronger-backbone teacher is required for best results.
Primary benchmark is COCO only; VOC/BDD100K results in the appendix are single-run without repeated seeds or error bars, limiting confidence in generalization claims across datasets.

The comparison in Table 13 (longer schedules) showing baseline overfitting at 3x while DetGain keeps improving is presented somewhat one-sidedly; it is unclear whether standard regularization/LR adjustments for longer baseline schedules were applied, which could affect the fairness of this specific comparison.

Absolute mAP gains, while consistent, are moderate (~2-2.7 mAP on standard schedules), and the method introduces a fair amount of additional machinery (polynomial surrogate fits, dynamic ratio scheduling, augmentation pairing) that adds implementation complexity beyond the core idea.
